paras: The lynching of Calvin Moody was the hanging of a Black man accused of murdering his wife, carried out by a mob of about 200 Black men at Moulton, Lawrence County, Alabama, on the night of July 1, 1888, by most accounts. The mob overpowered the sheriff and a guard, took Moody from the jail, and hanged him from a tree outside town after he reportedly confessed. Wire reports printed across the country called it the first lynching in Alabama of a Black man by members of his own race.

According to a Birmingham dispatch, Moody quarreled with his wife on Friday night, June 29, over "a trifling matter," struck her on the head with a club, and stabbed her several times with a knife. The same dispatch said he dragged her into the woods near his house, where she bled to death, and afterward returned to cover her body with leaves. A dispatch from Hillsboro, Alabama, printed in the Memphis Appeal, told it differently: it described the wife as pregnant, placed the killing in woods two miles away, said her skull was crushed and her throat cut, and gave jealousy as the cause.
Moody was arrested on suspicion on Saturday morning, and his wife's body was found that afternoon.

On the night of the lynching, about 200 armed Black men surrounded the jail at Moulton. In the Birmingham account the sheriff and a special guard were overpowered, while the Hillsboro dispatch said the mob overpowered the jailer. The men carried Moody a short distance out of town and hanged him from a tree.

When the rope was thrown over the limb, the Birmingham account said, Moody asked for a chance to talk and made "a full confession of his crime." The Hillsboro dispatch also reported a confession and added that "the mob was orderly."
No report of an inquest, of arrests of mob members, or of grand jury action appears in the coverage, which ends in mid-July.

Most papers received the story as a brief Birmingham wire, which the St. Paul Daily Globe printed on July 4 as a special under the headline "Alabama's First Lynching." The Washington Evening Star ran it on July 5, as did the Maysville, Kentucky, Evening Bulletin under "Lynched by a Mob" and the Wahpeton Times in Dakota. Over the next ten days it reappeared in the Mitchell Capital and the Custer Chronicle in Dakota, the Abilene Weekly Reflector and the Iola Register in Kansas, and the Hillsboro News-Herald and Ohio Democrat, the last two under "Lynched For Wife Murder." Its whole point was the race of the mob: the lynching, it said, "was done by a mob of 200 negroes, and is the first case of the kind in this state."

A fuller Birmingham account dated July 4 appeared in the Atlanta Constitution's Alabama news column on July 10 and in the Emporia Weekly News on July 12, where it was headed "An Exclusively Black Lynching." That version opened by calling the event "the first lynching of a negro by men of his own race" in the state and relayed the confession without question. The Memphis Appeal alone characterized Moody in its headline, "A Negro Brute Lynched," and none of the reports carried editorial comment.

Reports differed on the night of the lynching: most printings of the short wire and the Hillsboro dispatch said Sunday night, July 1, while the Evening Star's version said Saturday night, June 30. The Emporia printing of the fuller account said Sunday in its first sentence but Saturday for the attack on the jail, whereas the Atlanta Constitution's printing of the same text said Sunday in both places. Because the wife's body was found only on Saturday afternoon and the independent Hillsboro dispatch also gave Sunday, Sunday night has the stronger support.
The mob numbered 200 in most papers but 500 in the Wahpeton Times and the Mitchell Capital, both printings of the same short wire.

accounts.label: Birmingham wire, short version
accounts.gist: Moody, colored, was lynched at Moulton by a mob of 200 negroes for the murder of his wife the previous Friday night; the first case of the kind in the state.

accounts.label: Birmingham wire, fuller version
accounts.gist: Moody killed his wife with a club and knife after a trifling quarrel and hid her body; arrested Saturday, he was taken from the jail by about 200 armed negroes who overpowered the sheriff and a guard, and hanged after making a full confession.

accounts.label: Hillsboro, Ala., dispatch
accounts.gist: Moody, out of jealousy, took his pregnant wife to woods two miles off, crushed her skull and cut her throat; 200 colored men overpowered the jailer Sunday night and hanged him; he confessed and the mob was orderly.

framing.detail: The short wire ran under 'Alabama's First Lynching', 'Lynched by a Mob', 'Lynched For Wife Murder' and 'Lynched.', stressing that the mob was Black and that it was the first case of the kind in the state, with no comment.
The fuller account, headed 'An Exclusively Black Lynching' in Emporia, called it 'the first lynching of a negro by men of his own race' in Alabama and relayed the confession as fact.
The Memphis Appeal headlined 'A Negro Brute Lynched' and closed by noting 'The mob was orderly.'

versions.value: Both: Sunday night in the lead, Saturday night for the jail siege

conflicts.note: Sunday has the most support: it appears in most wire printings, in the independent Hillsboro dispatch, and in the Atlanta printing of the fuller account, which uses Sunday in both places; the body was found only Saturday afternoon.
The 500 figure appears only in two reprints of the same short wire, most likely a typesetting variant.
